newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai election news buoys stocks, baht - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Thai election news buoys stocks, baht - analysts.

text.p: Money market dealers said on Monday that the snap Thai election set for November 17 would boost baht stability and induce foreign capital inflows as the Thai stock market rallied sharply on the news.

The dealers said Singapore currency traders sold forward dollar/baht swap contracts in favour of the Thai unit on Monday morning, reflecting confidence that post-election Thai politics would give the country a more qualified economic team to handle its problems.
Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa dissolved his 14-month coalition on Friday and called the early election after his partners tried to force him to resign.

"The general feeling is that politics is changing for the better. Unless there's a big election upset, Thailand should have a government more capable of handling economic problems," said a dealer at Citibank.

The Thai bourse, hammered for several months on weak Thai economic indicators and political uncertainty, rallied sharply on Monday morning, surging 48.91 points, or 4.67 percent, in reaction to Banharn's election decision.
"Investors are happy this government will depart after the general election that will allow a new government to rule the country," said Thanawat Patchimkul of Seamico Securities.
The Thai overnight interbank rate eased to 12.25-12.50 percent on Monday morning from 13.00 late on Friday. Bank dealers said local money market liquidity was partly boosted by foreign funds.
A dealer at HongKong and Shanghai Bank said the overnight interbank rate may ease further to about 11.00 percent in one or two weeks.
"The market this morning indicated initial positive reaction to changing Thai politics. The interbank rates are heading down," he said.

Another dealer at Thai Military Bank Plc said the Thai overnight rate did not fall sharply on Monday because of a firmer U.S. dollar that prompted some market players to speculate in favour of the U.S. unit.

Dealers said Banharn's last administrative decision before he dissolved his coalition on Friday, in naming deputy central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswadsi as caretaker deputy finance minister, would boost confidence in the baht's stability.
They said Chaiyawat was the top central bank official in charge of Thai intervention in local and regional markets to defend the baht in late July and early August.

"It should put to rest any doubt about what the authorities would do (to defend the baht) unless new Thai economic indicators in the next one or two months turn out to be worse than expected," the Citibank dealer said.

Sporadic baht attacks in July and August were triggered by market rumours that Thailand may choose to devalue the baht to help its sluggish exports, which grew only 2.9 percent during January/July against 26.5 percent a year ago.
Private economists projected that Thailand's gross domestic product would expand at a 10-year low of about 7.0 percent this year against 8.6 percent in 1995.
Pressure on the baht halted a heavy inflow of short-term foreign funds seen early this year.
Thailand's outstanding short-term foreign loans channelled through offshore banking units posted a decline for the first time in July.
